Preface
Criterion-referenced assessments evaluate a student’s performance against a set of predetermined criteria or standards. In contrast, norm-referenced assessments compare a student’s performance to the performance of a larger group, typically their peers. Criterion-referenced assessments are used to determine whether a student has mastered a specific set of skills or knowledge, while norm-referenced assessments are used to rank students against each other. This book focuses on criterion-referenced assessments, which are commonly used in educational settings to measure student learning and inform instruction (Furtado, 2004)
Criterion-referenced assessments are used to evaluate student performance on specific learning objectives, such as the ability to solve a particular type of math problem or to write a coherent essay. These assessments are designed to measure what students know and can do, rather than how they compare to their peers. Criterion-referenced assessments are used to determine whether students have met specific learning objectives, and to provide feedback to students and teachers on areas where improvement is needed. This book provides an overview of criterion-referenced assessments, including their purpose, design, and implementation. It also includes examples of criterion-referenced assessments in various subject areas, as well as tips for creating and using these assessments in the classroom.

title: 1  Overview
section: 1.2 The Importance of Fundamental Movement Skill Development
text:
1.2 The Importance of Fundamental Movement Skill Development
Fundamental movement skill (FMS) development in children is important to their overall development and well-being. FMS skills are basic movements like running, jumping, and throwing that use the large muscles in the body (Furtado and Gallagher 2012). These skills are crucial for physical, cognitive, and social development

Physical activity and health: Mastering fundamental motor skills, like those categorized as stability, locomotion, or object manipulation, is linked to greater participation in sports and physical activities later in life. Children with good gross motor skills are more likely to be physically active and healthy. For example, one study showed that object control proficiency in childhood predicted higher levels of moderate-to-vigorous and organized physical activity in adolescence.

Cognitive development: Some research suggests that gross motor development may be related to cognitive development. While more research is needed on this connection, improved physical activity through gross motor skills can increase blood flow and oxygen to the brain. This may help with concentration, memory, and problem-solving.

Social development: Gross motor skills enable children to play with others, participate in group activities, and build relationships. This social interaction helps children develop confidence, cooperation, and communication skills. They can also experience a sense of belonging and learn about teamwork.


It is important to note that gross motor skills do not develop automatically, and they need to be nurtured, promoted, and practiced. Children need opportunities to play and explore their environment to develop these skills. Parents, educators, and caregivers can encourage gross motor development by providing safe and stimulating environments.
Targeting fundamental motor skills in childhood interventions, particularly those aimed at promoting long-term physical activity, is a key strategy for better health and well-being.
